newsitem.title: USA: North Dakota town watches water surround it.
newsitem.headline: North Dakota town watches water surround it.

text.p: They closed the last road out of Harwood Thursday.

This town of 590 a few miles north of Fargo became a prisoner of the Sheyenne River shortly after noon when Interstate 29, the main route north to Canada's prairie provinces and south to the U.S. heartland, was cut off by rising waters.
The southbound lanes were already covered for about a mile by water deep enough to lick the undercarriages of passing cars.
The town itself and those who chose to remain there were dry, hiding behind an elaborate earthen dike dug up in massive chunks from the black dirt of surrounding farm fields.

Dallas Marohl, a member of town's flood committee which started building the dikes three weeks ago, said there have been "no serious problems" in the village so far. There were some reports of water in garages, he said, but no more than usual with spring snowmelt flooding.
Snow from a record winter's accumulation was still piled high in yards.

"I'm very confident that we'll pull through this and not let anything happen within the city limits," he told Reuters. "Outlying houses in the rural areas have been flooded and unfortuantely those people have had to evacuate."
Marohl said some residents had left Harwood but there were no plans to evacuate the town. The school has been closed and students sent to Fargo and West Fargo for classes.
"There isn't a word great enough to describe the community support," he said.

Bernie Stasch, Harwood's superintendent of public works, said the water was not expected to crest until the middle of next week. Anyone electing to stay in town, he said, had already been told to stock enough supplies to last a week or two.

The Sheyenne, which passes west of town on the other side of the interstate highway, is a winding, shallow stream that eventually empties into the Red River of the North, several miles east of Harwood.
It has spilled out of its banks gently but persistently, covering the flat, frozen farm fields.

Harwood is typical of many towns in the Red River Valley, a vast tabletop region slightly tilted toward Canada. With no deep valleys gouged in the plain, the floodwaters are likely spread far and wide as they flow northward, turning thousands of acres between Fargo and Winnepeg, Manitoba, into lakes.
In an emergency, someone could be taken to or from Hardood by helicopter, boat or perhaps a military-type vehicle. But for now the usual way of coming and going was gone.
"We're isolated now. We're stuck until its over," said a clerk at the town offices.
